sections.title: Rubber compound options
sections.live: LIVE → Neoprene, SBR — two of the eight · natural rubber, the compound a suspension stop is normally made from, is not offered

fields.label: All eight, always — and the omission here is the important one
paragraphs: Margo produces every part in every compound it mixes (client-instructed 2026-09-02). The live selector offers two, understating the offer by six.

🛑 On a load-bearing suspension stop, natural rubber is not a preference — it is the normal answer. Highest fatigue life and lowest creep of the eight, which is exactly what a part that carries a laden chassis and then absorbs the strike needs. It is not on this page.

And SBR, which is offered, is wrong twice over here: lower fatigue life than natural rubber, and poor ozone resistance on a part bolted to a chassis that lives outdoors in monsoon and dust. Ozone cracking is the documented failure mode of a solid rubber stop.

fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: A commercial stop is loaded on every rough surface, not twice a year. Fatigue life governs, which is why natural rubber — not the cheapest compound — is the right specification.
Free height and static load, not hardness. A stop that sets loses height and starts striking earlier and harder every trip. Send the load, the height and the strike energy.
Most commercial stops are rubber on a steel bracket or stud. We mould and bond in one process under one set of batch records — no external toolmaker, no split responsibility for the bond.
Compounded for the chassis, not the lab
Natural rubber is right for the load and vulnerable to ozone. We compound it with an anti-ozonant system for chassis exposure rather than switching to a weaker compound.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change and no new element.
Card 03 is the commercial one on this page. The OEM description says “Assy.” — this is a bonded part — and an aftermarket supplier who can ship the assembly rather than the rubber alone takes the whole line item.
Card 04 is the technical one, and it is the argument a buyer will not have heard. The obvious move when a natural-rubber part cracks is to switch compound. The right move is to compound the natural rubber properly, and saying so is the clearest signal on this page that Margo mixes its own rubber rather than buying it in

notes: This is the page’s AEO asset — everything else is shared with 30 other URLs.
Moulding process, named per part: compression moulded, transfer where the bracket is bonded in. Correct here.
🛑 Do not repeat SKU 03’s polyurethane boundary on this page. It applies to passenger-car jounce bumpers; a CV suspension stop is solid rubber and squarely in scope.

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.chip: Keep · correct process for this part
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · “compression moulding” is right on this page

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. Anti-ozonant loading is set here, which is what makes a natural-rubber chassis part survive.
Mould design & CNC — precision steel tooling manufactured in-house and held as a controlled record. [no change]
Compression and transfer moulding — hydraulic press cycles at controlled temperature and pressure. Transfer where the steel bracket is bonded in, which is how this part is built
Post-cure & trimming — oven post-cure for dimensional stability, followed by flash trimming. Post-cure matters on a load-bearing part: an under-cured stop creeps.
Quality inspection — dimensional check, hardness testing and batch sampling before release. Free height and bond integrity are what is checked.

Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used. Stops are packed loose, since rubber stored under load takes a set before it is ever fitted.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept — the template’s process is right here. Four steps gain a part-specific reason.
Step 01 carries the argument from section 04 card 04, and it is the only place on the site where compounding is described as a decision rather than a step. Step 05’s bond-integrity check is the one an aftermarket buyer will ask about, because a debonded stop is a warranty return

notes: The process block must render from the part record even where the default is correct.
Numbered steps are an <ol>.
“Bond integrity” and “anti-ozonant” are technical terms worth carrying — they are what a CV parts buyer uses and neither appears anywhere on this site.
